1:
Matthew Henry sets the habit before the instance: pressed by neighbours on one side, the people had a way of seeking help from neighbours on the other rather than looking up to God, and here, threatened by the Assyrians, they sought the Egyptians and were taunted with it by the enemy’s own officer. He brings two counts. They would not consult God, being so confident in the prudence of their own measures that they thought it needless and were unwilling to put the matter to that test; they take counsel among themselves and cover themselves with a shelter not of his Spirit, which will prove too short a covering, a refuge of lies. And they could not confide in God, not thinking it enough to have him on their side, but strengthening themselves in the strength of Pharaoh.

The covering is disputed. Adam Clarke renders the Hebrew as who pour out a libation, since libation was constantly used in ratifying covenants, so that it stands for a covenant as one Greek word does for the same reason; the Greek version renders it that they made covenants. Charles Ellicott prefers that weave a web, a phrase as fit now as then for double-dealing diplomacy, and reports a third rendering, that they form a molten image, meant not of idolatry but of trust in human plans. John Wesley keeps it simple: they seek a protection God never required, and to all their other sins add a distrust of his power and a confidence in an arm of flesh.

Ellicott hears the opening interjection as sorrow rather than indignation, and reads the whole as news: the intrigues of the palace have issued in favour of the alliance, an embassy has already gone, and it was done without consulting the recognised prophet. The strength of Pharaoh, he notes, is literally his fortress. John Gill surveys the datings on offer — a northern king who sent to Egypt, the times of a later prophet, another king at the end, and the reign of Ahaz, of which there is no record of such an embassy — and settles for Hezekiah, as the taunts delivered before the walls show.

John Calvin begins by conceding the objection: the reproof might seem excessively severe, since weak and oppressed men have a right to ask assistance even from wicked persons, nature having implanted the principle that human beings should help each other. But at the source there was no ordinary guilt: it is wicked obstinacy to despise God’s government and follow one’s own inclinations, and this alliance had been strictly forbidden. Of the two reasons for that prohibition he dwells on the general one, that God did not wish his people corrupted by the superstitions of the nations, since we are gradually infected by the vices of those we live among and are more prone by nature to copy vices than virtues. He offers his own country as the example, and traces the same immoderate desire for alliances in the opening of one continent and then another to a foreign power. He allows that we may use the services of men, but only so as to depend on God alone, and observes that the prophet sets Pharaoh over against God because creatures contend with God whenever men place their confidence in them.

On the third verse Calvin presses the outcome: the wicked are not merely disappointed of their hope but are labouring hard after their own ruin, and nothing acquired by unlawful methods can profit anyone. The strength of Pharaoh, he notes, is granted by way of concession, as if to say that what they took for protection will yield them nothing but reproach. Keil and Delitzsch mark a structural oddity: the address is barely under way when a heading appears of the kind used in the prophecies against the nations, which several critics dispose of by calling it spurious.
4:
Charles Ellicott reads the tenses as the historic present of prophecy, and places the two cities: the first among the oldest in Egypt, the second in the delta and among the first the embassy would reach. Adam Clarke reports that a dozen manuscripts and the Greek version read the second name not as a place but as the words in vain. John Calvin is interested in the cost: the alliance was bought with long journeys, much toil and vast sums, the envoys arriving loaded with presents at the most distant cities; and since those sent were princes, the censure is the heavier, for they solicited the alliance slavishly and wandered like suppliants.

The disappointment keeps the same tense. Ellicott says they found Egypt at once weak and false, without will or power to help, and sets beside it the enemy officer’s figure of a broken reed that pierces the hand leaning on it. Calvin explains the mechanism: God sometimes gives the wicked prosperity in order to punish them more severely, letting them be drawn on until they throw themselves down headlong; and he distinguishes two ways of failing, since the Egyptians might prove false, as men often forsake at the utmost need those they have fed with empty promises, or might try and still be useless, events being in God’s hand.

The heading in the sixth verse is a question. John Gill reports that some take it as beginning a new prophecy and serving as its title. Clarke denies there is room for a new title, takes the word as a load rather than an oracle, and asks whether it does not refer to the presents carried south; he identifies the country crossed with the deserts traversed at the exodus, of which they had been told they should return no more that way. Ellicott records the conjecture that the heading was a transcriber’s marginal note, prompted by the lions and camels below it, which later slipped into the text; but he sees no reason why the prophet should not have written it himself with the sarcasm of an indignant irony — you ask for an oracle, and you shall have one whose very heading condemns you — before going on with the journey through an arid south haunted by lions and venomous serpents, the asses and camels loaded with treasure to buy an alliance.

Calvin makes the same address a deliberate insult: the prophet turns from men to their pack animals because it was useless to speak to men deaf to every exhortation, and threatens that the effect of the prediction will reach the very beasts though the people do not understand it; their ardour was carried to such a pitch of madness that the tediousness of the journey did not discourage them.

The closing phrase is the chapter’s best-known crux. Ellicott allows that our version fairly gives the meaning, that their boasted strength will prove absolute inaction, but says the words as spoken had an epigrammatic point our rendering loses: Rahab, they are sitting still, the poetical name for Egypt carrying the idea of haughty and inflated arrogance. It was, he says, almost a political caricature. Clarke arrives at nearly the same result by joining the last two words into one participle, so that the sense becomes Rahab the Inactive, and notes that a learned professor had published the same conjecture independently, a concurrence which adds to its probability. Calvin reads it as God’s complaint that his warnings produced no effect, since by sitting still they might have provided for their safety; John Wesley says it were safer to sit quietly at home and seek help from God. Keil and Delitzsch look forward to the command that follows, to write the oracle on a table, a separate leaf of durable material, and to do it in the people’s presence so that they might have it before their eyes.
8:
Matthew Henry gives three reasons for the writing. It is to shame the men of the present age, who would not hear it spoken, so their children may profit though they will not; to justify God in the judgments about to fall, since people would think him too severe unless they knew how provoking the nation was; and to warn others, even in the remotest age, not to do as they did lest they fare as they fared. He notes the care taken over the medium, not loose papers which might be lost but a table hung up for public view and a book preserved for posterity, and draws the moral for ministers, that it may be of use not only to preach but to write, since what is written remains.

John Calvin supplies the practice behind the command. It was customary for the prophets to fix an abridgment of their discourses to the gates of the temple; after all had been given time to read it, the ministers took it down and kept it among the temple records, and in that way the book of the prophets was collected. A weighty prediction, he adds, God commanded to be written in larger characters, that people might read it more attentively. Calvin then draws out the cost to the writer: there is nothing men resent more than having their crimes published and fastened on the remembrance of later ages, so that this prophecy must have earned its author the hatred of every rank.

The details are disputed. John Gill allows the thing written to be either their sins or the prophecy of their destruction, and thinks both may be meant, describing the table as wood covered with wax and hung against a wall. Adam Clarke prefers for a testimony for ever to for ever and ever, four versions supporting him and two Greek words having dropped out of the remaining copies. Charles Ellicott takes the command as passing into an act before the prophet’s astonished hearers, and reads it as his own sense that what he is about to say goes beyond the occasion; but he reports a rival construction, following the Latin, which turns the verb into an imperative and gives, they are boasters, cease from them. John Wesley notes only that it was to be written twice, for the present and for posterity.

What was written is a demand, and Keil and Delitzsch translate it without varnish: the people forbid the seers to prophesy straight or true things, meaning things not agreeable to their own wishes, and ask instead for what is smooth and flattering, and even for illusions. Ellicott makes the same point about their motive: not knowing the law of right themselves, they wished the seers to be as blind as they were, and would have had the prophets tune their voices to the time.

Ellicott hears something particular in the last clause. It seems as though the repeated utterance of that one divine title caused a bitterness of irritation which the more familiar names did not, because it made men feel they stood face to face with an infinite holiness, and this they could not bear. Calvin reaches the same place by another road: wicked men do not merely ridicule the doctrine but drive it furiously away and would have it crushed and buried, the power of the word wounding them until they give vent to their fierceness like wild beasts. He adds that the prophet is not quoting anyone: these were cunning hypocrites who boasted of worshipping God and complained of being unjustly reproached, far too clever to say such things aloud, so that what is given is their actual disposition with the mask torn off. And he concludes: to set the prophets aside is to set God aside, since God wills to be heard through those he charged with declaring his will.
12:
John Gill notices that the message is introduced with the very title the people had asked to be rid of, and draws a rule: ministers must not drop a phrase because natural men dislike it, but inculcate it the more. Charles Ellicott makes the same observation, that the prophet enforces his message as coming from precisely that Holy One of whom they were tired of hearing. Adam Clarke proposes reading obliquity for oppression, on a transposition of two letters he calls very probable, while John Calvin takes the disputed noun as robbery, rejects the rendering calumny as too weak, and applies it not to unlawful wealth but to the rebelliousness in which the nation indulged.

The bulging wall is worked by everyone. Clarke supplies the building practice: the houses of that region are little better than mud walls, one traveller reporting a city built of bricks of clay and straw dried in the sun, which the least rain dissolves, another that walls of earth often cleave from top to bottom. Ellicott suggests the half-decayed houses of the city furnished the picture, and lays out three stages, the bulge, the crack, the crash. Calvin turns the image into a moral: a wall swells because its parts no longer hold together, so the haughtiness of wicked men is itself the surest proof that ruin is near, the more they are puffed up without solid worth the faster they go down by their own weight. Wesley puts it in a line, a high wall bulging in places, which the least accident brings down.

The potter’s vessel raises the stakes. Calvin observes that a fallen wall leaves stones that can be used again, whereas broken pottery cannot be mended, so the threat takes away every hope of restoration — needed, since nothing is harder than rooting false confidence out of men cast down twice and three times who still raise their crests. Ellicott adds that these schemes were to be not merely crushed but pulverised.

The refused remedy is put positively first. Ellicott reads returning and rest as a conversion whose character the context fixes: a turning from trust in man, with all its restless excitement, to a trust in God full of calmness and peace. Calvin explains why the prophet descends to one instance: warnings in general terms leave hypocrites room to protest that they never rejected the word, whereas by naming the case he asks why, when God had said their strength lay in hope and silence, they raised a commotion instead.

The refusal is answered by a play on words. Calvin admires the throwing back of their own phrase, since to flee in their mouths meant to escape and in the answer means to take flight: you shall flee, not to find refuge but to turn your back and be chased by horses swifter than your own. Ellicott identifies the horses as the expected Egyptian contingent, on whose fame the generals were reckoning, and observes that the prophet, knowing the real temper of Egypt, says they will serve only for a quicker retreat. Keil and Delitzsch read the same reversal and carry it into the promise that follows.

On the rout the notes divide between text and picture. Clarke argues that a word has dropped out of the second line, answering to the thousand of the first; the Greek supplies many, but two passages in the law show the true word to be ten thousand. Ellicott grants the hyperbole is common, but notes that an Egyptian king’s inscription boasts of his strength in the self-same words, which may sharpen the sarcasm. He corrects the beacon to a pine, and finds two emblems of solitariness, the tall pine alone on a height and the flag-staff seen far off against the sky. Calvin adds that numbers and fortresses avail nothing when the heart fails; Wesley says only, till few of you are left.
18:
Matthew Henry reads the turn as an antithesis: notwithstanding all that has just been threatened, yet will the Lord wait. Having shown that those who trusted Egypt would be ashamed, he shows that those who sat still and trusted God would have the comfort of it; all will be well yet with those that fear God. Henry glosses the waiting three ways: God waits till they return and seek his face, and is then ready to meet them with mercy; he waits so as to give it at the fittest time, when it comes with the most pleasing surprise; and he continually follows them with favours. John Gill presses the verb, which he says carries a sense of panting and longing; God waits for the worst extremity, when his people feel their danger and their sins, so that the mercy is the sweeter.

Charles Ellicott puts the same thought in a proverb, that man’s extremity is God’s opportunity, and takes the waiting as a longing with eager expectation to come to the rescue; the waiting of the last clause, he adds, is the same wistful longing on the other side. He would also emend: a slight alteration turns he will be exalted into he will wait in stillness, and the God of judgment is better a God of righteousness.

Adam Clarke reaches nearly the same place by manuscript evidence, reporting a conjecture that reads he shall be silent for he shall be exalted, which one manuscript supports while another gives he shall return; the confusion of two similar letters, he notes, often breeds such mistakes. John Calvin keeps the received text but insists that judgment denotes not punishment only but the moderation exercised in chastening, as when another prophet asks to be chastened in judgment and not in wrath, God observing a limit in punishing those whose salvation he is always promoting. Calvin also sets this waiting against the excessive haste rebuked at the chapter’s opening: the Lord does not render like for like, and will not hurry to punish as they hurried to save themselves. John Wesley compresses it: God patiently expects their repentance and will work gloriously.

The promise gets a text-critical shaking. Clarke argues that a word has fallen out and should be restored from the Greek, so that the line reads when a holy people shall dwell in Zion, which clears a sense otherwise extremely obscure, and he recalls that when the other cities were taken this one was preserved with all in it. He also doubts the negative in the next clause, since the Greek lacks it and the word may be a mistake for another differing only slightly, giving thou shalt implore him with weeping. Ellicott, keeping the text, observes that the two place-names are practically synonymous and that the prophet lingers on both out of a patriot’s affection.

On what the promise contains they converge. Keil and Delitzsch describe the heirs of the grace that follows the judgment: a people newly pardoned in answer to its own cry for help, led by faithful teachers in the right way, and renouncing its idols with disgust. Calvin thinks the promise would have seemed incredible after so complete a desolation, yet holds that the Church is preserved, and insists the mourning is not perpetual, since they who sow in tears shall reap in joy, though he grants how hard it is to taste consolation while the mind is overwhelmed by a conviction of God’s vengeance. Gill takes the verse as counsel to stay put, waiting God’s time rather than running to Egypt. Wesley dates the fulfilment twice over, partly in the return from captivity and more fully in gospel times. Henry looks past both to the Zion above, where they will weep no more for ever, and adds that even now they would have more comfort if they were more constant in prayer.
20:
The commentators split on a single word. Charles Ellicott renders the opening better as bread in small quantity and water in scant measure, hearing the scant rations of the siege Jerusalem was to endure, and finds the compensation in the teachers: the true ones, no longer thrust into a corner as under Ahaz, would at last be recognised. He knows a variant reading the singular, thy teacher, meaning God himself, but prefers the plural, and points to a later embassy in the book as a virtual fulfilment. John Calvin will not have it. Some take the word for a teacher, he says, but this does not agree with the context; the multitude was more deeply affected by the want of food, and the prophet accommodates his language to their ignorance, giving a taste of God’s fatherly kindness under the emblem of abundance. Bread and water here mean extreme want, and instead of that famine God will send plenty. Calvin also reads the conjunction as when or after, so that the promise follows the endured chastisement rather than cancelling it. Adam Clarke keeps to the manuscripts, reporting that sixteen copies and three editions replace the divine title with the covenant name, as do all his own. John Gill takes the adversity historically, of the present siege or the later one by the Chaldeans, or of a famine such as sieges bring, and then extends it to the afflicted state of God’s people in the first times of the Gospel.

On the voice behind, Gill collects the pictures: schoolmasters who stand at their scholars’ backs, shepherds who call back a sheep that strays, travellers halted at a fork and called to from behind. He canvasses the identifications too, the reading the Jews give, the reading that makes it conscience, his own preference for the Spirit, and settles on the Scriptures as the only rule of faith and practice. John Wesley takes it for the voice of God’s word and Spirit, and keeps the shepherd metaphor. Ellicott makes the outer and the inner voice one thing: the human teacher on whom the people looked would find an echo within. Calvin makes this the greater of the two promises, since no scarcity of wheat should alarm us like a scarcity of the word, and the false prophets boast of the word more haughtily than godly teachers do; God must give the ears as well as the word, or he speaks to the deaf. Clarke again reports a variant, that three old versions translate as though they read a negative in place of the particle, giving turn not aside to the right or the left.

The idols go last. Gill sees images of solid silver decked in costly garments, or wooden ones plated with silver, not merely defaced but defiled, to show contempt. Wesley glosses the covering as the plates and the ornament as a costly robe. Ellicott reads the putting away of the besetting sin as the first effect of the turning, takes the graven image for a carved wooden figure afterwards overlaid, and notes that what had been worshipped was to be cast out like the very type of loathsomeness. Clarke hears the prohibition of Moses thrown out of prose into poetical form. Calvin presses the public act: since statues are the instruments of superstition, the truly converted abhor them and profane them so far as they can, as Jehu profaned the altars of Baal and turned that temple into a common sewer. Repentance is seated in the heart and has God for a witness, but it is shewn by its fruits, and the example is one godly princes and magistrates should follow. He guards the word profaned: the idols were never sacred, for nothing that dishonours God can be, but men falsely imagine they possess some sacredness, and so they are to be rejected as things of no value and altogether unclean.
23:
Keil and Delitzsch track the shape: the promise, after the act of penitence, rises higher and higher, and would not stop at bread in time of need. John Calvin reads the same ascent morally. The fruit of repentance is that God receives the converted into favour and loads them with blessings; but because he had begun out of order, with earthly and fading things, the prophet now adds to doctrine, the spiritual nourishment, what belongs to this corruptible life. Godliness has the promise of both lives, yet first aims at heaven. Hence, he adds, it is vain to toil in cultivating fields if the Lord sends no rain, and if the produce is abundant the glory is his. Charles Ellicott hears the prophet following an earlier one, drawing outward plenty as the sequel to the renewal of the nation’s inner life. John Gill keeps it agricultural: rain to the seed once sown, causing it to take root. John Wesley notes the bread is the fruit of their own land and labour, excellent and abundant.

The provender draws out the chapter’s closest philology. Ellicott reminds the reader that to ear the ground means to plough it, and renders the clean provender literally salted— the favourite mash of the best-fed cattle, corn mixed with salt or alkaline herbs, not inferior barley and chopped straw but the finest winnowed grain; that even the lowlier asses got it was the last word in plenty. Wesley makes the same point plainly: corn instead of straw, and pure grain at that. Calvin takes the verse as repetition drawn from the Law, quoted gladly by the prophets so that we may discern the indignation of God in the sickness and death of cattle. Gill notes the two beasts, unyoked but used separately in ploughing.

On the streams upon the high hills the readings divide by temperament. Calvin insists the language is allegorical, accommodated to our ignorance: the prophets describe the kingdom of Christ with metaphors from ordinary life because our minds cannot comprehend the blessings, and we must not judge that happiness by outward abundance, which believers often lack. The image strikes by its impossibility: water is not plentiful on peaks exceedingly dry. Ellicott keeps the golden age in view but ties it to history: the day of great slaughter falls perhaps on the enemies of Israel, perhaps on the people themselves, and the towers are either those they trusted in or those of the besiegers. Adam Clarke would emend that word: for the towers he reads the mighty, on the evidence of two old versions and the Chaldee. Wesley reaches the same sense unemended, taking the towers for mighty potentates; Gill sets the hills round about Jerusalem.

The sevenfold light closes the promise, and here two of them agree against the text. Clarke calls the comparison to the light of seven days a manifest gloss taken in from the margin, absent from most copies of the Greek and obscuring the sense; Keil and Delitzsch report that modern commentators from Lowth downwards mostly say the same, and grant one external witness for it. Calvin keeps it and reasons from nature: the brightness of the sun was never increased, not when it stood still for Joshua nor when the dial went backward for Hezekiah; the prophet speaks not of prolonging its course but of increasing its light, for those who alone share this happiness. Gill hears hyperbole for the light of the Gospel surpassing the former dispensation, and reports the Jews, Kimchi among them, referring it to the days of the Messiah. Ellicott sees the vision ascend from the new earth to the new heaven, and hears the apostle’s logic: if one is the reconciling of the world, what shall the other be but life from the dead. Wesley reads the healing as making the two kingdoms one, and Jew and Gentile one fold under one shepherd.
27:
The chapter turns to the Assyrian, and John Gill reads all that follows as the destruction of that army and a type of the destruction of antichrist; the name of the Lord is the Lord himself, or else the angel who came in that name and destroyed the host, said to come from far because he came from heaven. John Wesley makes it an earnest of the greater mercies promised. Charles Ellicott finds more in the circumlocution: the use of the Name for God himself anticipates the later memra of the Targumim and the word of St. John, a distinct though undefined conception of a duality in the divine essence. John Calvin explains the same usage from the polemic. The Assyrians worshipped gods of gold and silver and ridiculed the Jews for worshipping under no image or statue, one writer saying they worship the bright clouds and the deity of the sky; wicked men judge of God by outward appearances, think him at a great distance, and mock the confidence of believers as groundless, so the prophet adapts his language to their view and shews that the God they thought far off is at hand. Keil and Delitzsch see two figures melted together, a storm rising from the farthest horizon that turns the sky into a sea of fire, and a man burning with wrath whose lips foam and whose tongue moves like a flame; Adam Clarke renders the heavy burden as the flame raging violently.

Matthew Henry catalogues the instruments. The overflowing stream reaches the neck and overwhelms the whole army, while its head escapes to be struck later in the house of his god; the sieve is one of vanity, which retains nothing, and they are found all chaff; the bridle forces them to methods destructive to themselves, so that God guides his people with a word but turns his enemies headlong with a bridle. Henry also hears the indignation directed at the blasphemy of Rabshakeh, who compared the God of Israel with the gods of the heathen. Clarke reconstructs the winnowing from Kimchi: the van was a large instrument like a shovel with a long handle, with which corn mixed with chaff was tossed into the air for the wind to separate; but this van is one of emptiness, leaving nothing useful behind. He notes the irregular verb form, a proposed misdivision of the words, and that of the ancient versions only the Vulgate caught the sense, reducing the nations to nothing, though it dropped the image. Ellicott prefers the winnowing fan of nothingness and reads the bridle as a constraining power leading the enemy against his will to his own destruction, whom God would destroy being first driven mad. Wesley presses that it is no ordinary sieve, casting away the chaff only, but one that shakes until all is cast away.

The song divides them. Ellicott takes the holy solemnity for the Feast of Tabernacles, the most joyful of the year, with its night ritual and the temple court lit by a great candelabrum, and hears in the second clause the day ritual of pilgrims coming up with firstfruits and flutes; Keil and Delitzsch and Wesley hear the passover instead, the former arguing from the mention of the night and reading the whole as a counterpart of the deliverance from Egypt. Gill recalls the song at the drowning of Pharaoh in the Red Sea. Calvin guards the joy: it is called holy because joy that does not look straight towards God is fruitless and irreligious, and they shall not dance as irreligious men do; the mountain is the temple, and the title Rock reminds them that when we cherish a conviction of our own strength we rob God of it. Henry says the same more shortly: our joy in the fall of the enemies of the church must be a holy joy.
30:
The voice is heard first. John Gill renders it the glory of his voice and takes it, with the Targum, for the word that gave the order the angel obeyed; it is commonly read of thunder, and the destruction may well have come by thunder and hail, though the history omits it. John Wesley agrees that the thunder stands for some terrible judgment, and Charles Ellicott sets the peace at home against the full thunderstorm falling on the enemy, hailstones and coals of fire being the natural symbols of anger. Keil and Delitzsch catch the contrast: Israel marches joyfully to a sacred and glorious height while outside God sweeps the world-power entirely away, without any help from Israel. John Calvin asks why the threat needed repeating, and answers from human dullness. When God delays we think him asleep or not powerful; and even when we see his judgments we keep masks before us, ascribing them to fortune or to the plans of men. So the event will be made so manifest that none can fail to see that the calamity proceeded from the mouth, that is the decree, of God. Adam Clarke stays with the manuscripts, weighing swift anger against indignant detestation, and notes that the common reading appears in no Bible before 1705, where it looks like a printer’s mistake.

The rod itself is the chapter’s worst crux. Clarke says no one has yet made tolerable sense of the grounded staff, and reports a conjecture giving the rod of correction, found in two manuscripts, beside an old version reading the taming rod. Ellicott, equally blunt that the English is unclear, offers the destined rod, literally the rod of foundation. Wesley keeps the founded rod, founded because firmly established by God’s immutable purpose. Calvin takes the fastening physically, from strokes so heavy that the mark of the instrument remains, as though the staff stuck in the wound; wherever it passes it sticks fast, and there is no retreat. Gill has the same image, a staff fastened in the earth. Calvin adds why the Assyrian must fall: the measure he meted is measured to him again, and though he seemed too strong to fall, God needs no arms but his voice; believers are not to ask how, but to rest on the bare promise.

The music at each stroke draws a striking parallel from Ellicott: Israel raises its song with the timbrels and harps used after victory, and recalls that the long walls joining Athens to the Piraeus were pulled down by the Spartans to the sound of music; he reads the battles of shaking as battles of swinging, the action of a warrior swinging his sword to and fro. Clarke would read against them for against it, on fifty-two manuscripts and five editions.

Tophet closes it. Gill and Clarke agree on the valley of the son of Hinnom outside Jerusalem: Gill derives its name from the drums beaten there to drown the cries of the children offered to Molech, and notes that the word for hell comes from it; Clarke adds that in the Gospel it stands for hell-fire, and that the name is used by metonymy, the army having probably been destroyed further off, on the other side of the city. Ellicott hears sarcasm in the Hebrew, where the phrase for the king suggests the god worshipped there, so the great sacrifice is of the king to Moloch, and the deep wide trench and mighty pyre are what such a funeral required. Keil and Delitzsch translate it as a place for the sacrifice of abominations long made ready. Calvin will not have a place at all: Tophet means hell, and we must not fancy some prison in which the wicked are shut up; the name denotes their miserable condition, borrowed from the valley so that its bare mention might excite horror and make idolatry the more abhorred.
